# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):
- Dana Whitfield: HN/47279411 ("we wouldn't want to switch even for a higher yield… the operational burden is more important to us than yield", "about 3.2%"). The $300k transfer is **[author]**.
- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

whys.g1: Aisha and Lena both put insured, safe money first and belong together under a plain name, while my answer and Marcus's are about operational hassle, so they rightly stay out of that group and leaving them ungrouped is fair, even though a finance lead could see a shared low-hassle theme.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing needed keeping out.

whys.g1: Aisha's need for insured, explainable cash and my need to pull cash back fast sit naturally under a plainly named group, Marcus's paperwork and monthly-transfer complaint is about hassle and a better rate at the bank he already uses rather than reach or safety, and Rachel's runway and accountant point is its own reason, so leaving both ungrouped is right.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing was wrongly let into the group.

founder.order_why: Context, problem, solution and then the study setup is the sequence I'd expect, but screens 21 and 22 are labelled 'Interviews · Sent' while I'm still choosing how people answer and who gets a link.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('define exactly where this idea applies'), split only by the recency screen; I can only judge them by that heading.
founder.missing: Nothing asks about the commercial side: who pays and who decides (my founder signs off, while the finance lead moves the cash), whether a board, investor or tax adviser must agree, or what I charge, which is a flat 0.25% a year on balance rather than a monthly amount. It also doesn't ask about the risk being taken on, since the buyer's real question is whether principal can fall in a bond fund, which at 2 days' liquidity and without FDIC cover is what could stop them moving the cash.

PRIMARY.order_why: The flow from screening to the idea makes sense, but the two-day wait question comes before I'm asked whether Palus would have helped or whether I'd move the reserve, so I'm judging a detail before the bigger question of whether the idea matters to me at all.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 5 and 7 partly overlap, since saying Palus wouldn't have made a difference already says much of why I wouldn't move the reserve, and the follow-ups on screens 6 and 8 draw on the same reasoning about operational burden.
PRIMARY.missing: What yield we earn today and how much more would make a switch worth it, plus how much operational burden we'd accept, such as approvals, onboarding, and keeping everything in one dashboard.

screens.instead: Keep the question and chip, but make the belief: 'For most, the cash from their last raise would have earned more with it: higher yield without hiring for treasury.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better than today, it's obvious why Keel shows me that claim back as the belief it will test.
screens.why2: Yield, treasury and the 1-in-3 bar are plain to me, but I had to reread "their last raise would have gone better with it" because it sounds like the fundraise itself went better, not where the cash sat afterwards.
screens.why3: I can judge this from what I know, because earning more on raise cash without a treasury hire is the claim I make, and I lived it with our own reserves.
screens.why4: The one row keeps my words, but it joins two different gains, higher yield and no treasury hire, so a "no difference" answer wouldn't show which one failed.
screens.why5: My label is intact, but Palus doesn't improve "their last raise"; it improves what the cash earns after the raise, so the framing has drifted from my claim.
screens.instead: For most, the cash from their last raise would have earned more with it, without hiring anyone for treasury. Bar: holds if no more than 1 in 3 say "no difference" or "worse".

screens.why1: Once I've said how it fits and what it does better, the obvious next question is what a finance lead has to do to get started, and I haven't been asked that yet.
screens.why2: The question and hint are plain on first read, and to me 'setup, extra steps or learning' clearly means linking Plaid and moving the reserve.
screens.why3: I built the onboarding and know exactly what it asks: link the bank through Plaid, then move the long-term cash across.
screens.why4: The only option is 'Leave this out of the study', a fair escape for a founder who doesn't want to test adoption effort, and the free-text box lets me give my true answer.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my words about moving the reserve but drops the Plaid link I typed, and 'Most would move' turns a required step into a prediction of what people would do.
screens.instead: Keep the question, hint and chip, but have Keel write: 'To start, most would have to link the company bank account through Plaid and move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what they must do to start, Keel shows the efforts it drafted and the one belief it will test, so it is obvious why I am checking this here.
screens.why2: Plaid, long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are everyday words to me and to the finance leads I sell to, and I understand each row on first reading.
screens.why3: These are the setup steps of my own product and I know the customer's side of them, so I can confirm them without guessing.
screens.why4: The steps are real and distinct, but they are out of order (opening the account comes first), 'treasury' means both the bank's product and ours, and moving the reserve misses startups whose cash sits in plain checking.
screens.why5: The rows match my Plaid connection and my claim that the problem is the bank's bundled treasury product, and the belief names the move I need them to make, leaving 'start small' to the commitment step.
screens.instead: Rows, in order: Open a Palus account in the company's name / Link the company bank account through Plaid / Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury or checking; belief: Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury or checking.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the steps to start, it is obvious why Keel asks which of them is the one to test as the riskiest belief, and this is the last of the four solution beliefs.
screens.why2: Plaid, treasury and long-term reserve are the words I use every day, and the belief reads clearly on first pass.
screens.why3: I know what onboarding asks of a customer and that moving the reserve is where they balk, since the thread told me so, so I can pick from what I know.
screens.why4: The three steps are distinct and in my words, but moving the reserve bundles the real commitment, while my advice to start small and grow the position over time has no option of its own.
screens.why5: The step is mine and the belief keeps its meaning, but 'most would move the long-term reserve' drifts a little from what I actually sell, which is starting small and growing the position.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but add the option 'Move a small part of the reserve first to try it', and let the belief read 'Most would move part of the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury.'

screens.why1: Right after I have defined the solution and before strangers see the study, deciding whether to ask for a real try is an obvious last setup choice.
screens.why2: Offer a pilot, leave your email, and the Pilot tab read clearly on first pass, though 'people who say yes' takes a moment to attach to the pilot line rather than to the study.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups from the people answering is entirely my own call, and I already tell founders to start small and try us out.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the whole decision, the two are distinct, and no escape chip is needed for a choice that is mine to make.
screens.why5: My real commitment step is to start small with part of the reserve, and 'try this for real' with an email is a looser ask than moving cash, though it does not contradict it.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, it makes sense to choose who will put my questions to people, and nothing earlier asked this.
screens.why2: The question and the choice are easy, but 'Tap the other face to hear her' and 'The voice goes with the face' take a second read, and the screen never says outright that an AI voice is doing the interview.
screens.why3: I can listen to two voices and pick the one I would want talking to a finance lead about their company's cash, and the credit cost is mine to weigh.
screens.why4: Two distinct named faces with a default already picked is a complete choice for this step, and no escape chip is needed because the link goes out by text either way.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed about Palus is changed here, and I simply keep the preselected face as I intended.
screens.instead: Who should interview people for you? Daphne is picked. Tap Saskia to hear her voice and switch. Keel records the voice you pick once for this project, which uses 400 credits, and people get the link by text either way.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, it is obvious why I am now choosing how people answer.
screens.why2: The question and the Text only option are plain, but the Daphne line 'Every answer in a quiet room. More than 9 in 10 where it is loud' is a clipped fragment that takes me a second read to see it means accuracy of capturing speech, and the stray word 'recording' is unexplained.
screens.why3: I know my finance leads and founders and can judge whether they would talk on video or tap and type about where the company's cash sits.
screens.why4: The three choices are complete and distinct and my pick is there, but the option text is untidy, with 'recording' left dangling after 'Hear it' and again after 'Let them choose', which reads like a broken label.
screens.why5: It is a study-delivery setting that does not touch my idea, and my Text only choice is offered as I would state it.
screens.instead: How should they answer? Options: Daphne, an AI interviewer (asks each question aloud on video; they talk, type or tap; catches nearly every spoken word in a quiet room and more than 9 in 10 in a loud one; hear a sample) / Text only (they read each question and tap or type) / Let them choose (they pick Daphne or text when they open the link).

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people answer, the last step before sending is deciding who receives the link, so the question is obviously in place.
screens.why2: "Who gets a link?" and the three options are plain to a startup founder on first reading; "Contacts page" is the only product term and its meaning is clear from context.
screens.why3: I know how I would reach finance leads and founders, whether through batchmates and people I know, a search, or a post in a founder group, so I can answer from what I actually do.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel-found list and one open link in a group are distinct, cover my real routes, and need no escape chip because this is a choice of sending method.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is offered in those words and kept as my answer, with nothing changed about my idea or roles.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' is plain, but no number sits beside it: the deciding 2 of 6 is down in card 2, and the line never says that adoption also failed at 2 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The counts and people are readable, but the base shifts from 7 to 6 without explanation, no card shows the bar it was judged against, and I need a second look at the '1 more only if' figures.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and all three belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, including 'higher yield without hiring for treasury'.
screens.why_b4: 'Fewer see a benefit than you think' is only a generic line: nothing tells me whether to rework the yield pitch, narrow to bigger reserves, or lower the effort of moving the reserve.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and the counts are honest, but the low n is never called low, 'fewer see a benefit than you think' generalises softly, and the count line's '1 people disagree' sits awkwardly against the card's 'Did not hold'.
screens.instead: Not holding up on 7 people, a small group: 6 of 7 could wait two days, but only 2 of 6 say their last raise would have gone better (the bar needed at least 4) and only 2 of 7 would move the reserve, so waiting isn't the obstacle; find out why the extra yield doesn't feel worth moving the money before building further.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said yes, easily or mostly", so I get the verdict and the number that decides it together, and they agree.
screens.why_b2: The counts and the 7 people are plain, but the bar line only repeats my belief without saying how many yeses it needs, and the names below use different words ("Yes, with some steps") from the bars ("Yes, mostly"), so I have to look twice.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and "they could wait two days for their cash" are the name and belief I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for Palus, such as treating the 1-2 day liquidity as no barrier and looking elsewhere for what is stopping people, or what to do about Lena's board, whose concern is insured money rather than timing.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible and no claim is made beyond those people, but "Holding up" against "most finance leads" never says 7 is a small group, which is a soft overstatement.
screens.instead: Holding up, among only 7 people: 6 of 7 could wait two days, and the bar was most of them. Waiting for cash isn't what will stop you, so don't spend effort on faster liquidity; Lena's objection is that the board wants the money insured, which is about safety, not timing.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits directly above "2 of 6 said it would have gone better", and that number plainly decides the verdict against my "most".
screens.why_b2: I can see at once that it counts better versus same over 6 people, but the bar line only repeats my claim, so I have to work out that no more than 1 in 3 was the limit and that 4 of 6 breaks it.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are the ones I checked, word for word, including "higher yield without hiring for treasury".
screens.why_b4: "Fewer see a benefit than you think" is generic, and although the quotes on access, paperwork and insurance point somewhere, the screen never says what this means for leading with yield.
screens.why_b5: The counts and the uncounted Rachel are visible and nothing is called strong, but "fewer see a benefit than you think" reads as a general claim from six people and the small n is never flagged.
screens.instead: Not holding up: only 2 of 6 said Palus would have made their last raise go better, and 4 said no difference where the bar allowed 2; this is a small sample, but those 4 cared about safety, insurance and easy access more than yield, so test leading with those before leading with yield.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "2 of 7 would do it", so I get the answer and the deciding number together, and they agree with my belief that most would move.
screens.why_b2: The bars plainly count people's answers and add up to 7, but the bar line only repeats my words, so I have to work out for myself that "most" is the bar and 2 of 7 falls short of it.
screens.why_b3: The Adoption friction name and the belief line are the ones I checked, down to "move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury".
screens.why_b4: The screen gives a result and quotes but never says what this means for Palus, so I have to work out for myself that fast cash access, paperwork and insurance are what to tackle.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n visible and claims nothing beyond the 7, but it never says 7 is a low count, and the one conditional answer is worded three ways ("clearly worth it", "cash back fast", and Aisha's quote wanting insured and easy to explain), so the "1 more" looks closer to a fast-cash yes than her words support.
screens.instead: Did not hold: only 2 of 7 finance leads, a small group, would move the reserve against your bar of most; 4 would not, citing access for monthly bills, paperwork and tax treatment, and 1 might if it were clearly worth it, so fix these objections or find who already wants to move before building on this belief.

screens.why_b1: Each line states its status word, but only Compatibility carries its deciding number (6 of 7) while Relative advantage and Adoption friction show just group counts that are not the 2 of 6 or 2 of 7 that decided them.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names are the ones I checked, but my belief lines (higher yield without hiring for treasury, moving the long-term reserve) are not on the screen, only the question headers, so I have to recognise them from memory.
screens.why_b4: The screen says nothing about what these results mean for Palus; I have to work out for myself that safety, insurance and easy access are what to answer next.
screens.why_b5: The counts are honest and small, but no line says n is low, and the same quotes reappear under different lines, so Aisha, Dana, Marcus and Lena can read like more voices than they are.
screens.why_b6: I typed yield and no hiring, and the quotes tell me what I did not write: the board asks why you lost money rather than why you earned less, monthly bills run out of treasury, a better rate inside the existing bank would have won, and the tax break pushes one accountant to plain cash.
screens.instead: Relative advantage, not holding up, 2 of 6: the four who saw no difference want insured money they can reach in two clicks and a better rate inside their own bank, so lead with safety and access, or offer the yield without a new account; only a handful answered, so test this with more finance leads.

screens.why1: As the first screen of a study about where a startup keeps its cash, it is obvious why they would check who I bank with before going further.
screens.why2: I can answer at once, but "a similar bank" needs a second thought because Mercury and Brex are fintechs rather than banks, and I would not call them that.
screens.why3: I run our accounts day to day, so I know exactly where we bank.
screens.why4: Yes and No are distinct and fit a gate with no escape, but a company using one of these alongside a traditional bank, or one unsure what counts as similar, has no clean fit between them.
screens.why5: It keeps to the Mercury, Brex or similar segment and leaks no product, plan or founder terms to me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options that I can hear once and answer, and naming the brands aloud is easy.
screens.instead: Does the startup you work at today keep its cash with Mercury, Brex or a similar startup-focused account? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: After checking where we bank, asking whether I actually made the call on raise cash recently is the obvious next gate.
screens.why2: I understand it straight away, but "sit" is loose because I mostly keep cash where it already is, and I can't tell if leaving it there counts as deciding.
screens.why3: Where our raise cash sits is my job, so I know whether I made that call in the last 3 months.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but "I can't recall one particular raise" doesn't fit a question about a 3-month window, and two escape chips is one too many for a gate that should have none.
screens.why5: It stays on where raise cash sits, and no product, plan or founder's term reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with a spoken yes or no and no escape read out, so I can hear it once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you decide where your startup's cash from a raise would be held, even if you chose to leave it where it was? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After two questions about where I bank and where I put the raise, showing me an idea to react to is the obvious next step and it is labelled as such.
screens.why2: Plaid, custodian and short-duration are all familiar to me, but 'the long-term reserve' assumes a bucket I may not have named and 'floating-rate, government-backed mortgage bonds' takes a second read to work out that this means agency MBS.
screens.why3: I hold raise cash and weigh yield against operational burden every day, so I can judge a linked account, the custody, the one-to-two-day return and the target against my 3.2 percent.
screens.why4: It is a card to read, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The card is an idea shown on purpose and stays a clear description with the belief credited to the people building it, with no leak of founder language about me or my role beyond the idea itself.
screens.why6: It says without symbols or parentheses, but 'short-duration, floating-rate, government-backed mortgage bonds' is a mouthful to catch on one hearing, and 'it would earn its target of 4.5 to 5 percent' comes out clumsily.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus. A treasury account linked to your existing bank through Plaid. It holds cash you won't need soon in a managed portfolio of short-term, government-backed mortgage bonds, held at a regulated custodian in your company's name. Cash returns to checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent.

screens.why1: Right after an idea card about where cash sits, asking whether a two-day wait for my money would work is the obvious next thing to test.
screens.why2: The words are simple, but "wait two days for your cash" doesn't say wait for what, since a raise isn't something I wait on day to day; I'd need a second read to get that it means pulling money out to my operating account.
screens.why3: I know our payroll and vendor rhythm well, but tying it to "your last raise" is odd because the need for same-day cash depends on the week rather than the raise, so I would partly guess.
screens.why4: "Yes, easily" and "Yes, mostly" sit close together and "mostly" doesn't fit a could-you-wait question well, though the range is covered and "I can't tell" fits.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the name on the card, but "Imagine Palus" tells me nothing on its own and the two-day wait arrives as a bare product term with no mention of a withdrawal or transfer, so the meaning has likely drifted.
screens.why6: It is two short sentences with one question and four short options plus one escape, easy to hold after hearing it once.
screens.instead: Think of your last raise. If moving that cash back to your operating account took two business days, would that have worked for you? Yes, easily; Yes, with some planning; Only sometimes; or No. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about waiting two days for my cash, it makes sense to ask whether this would have been better than what I did.
screens.why2: "Your last raise go better" makes me stop, because to me a raise is the fundraising round, and I have to work out that it means where the cash sat afterwards.
screens.why3: I know what we did with the cash and that switching has an operational cost, but I'd be partly guessing because I never used Palus and it had no bearing on how the round itself went.
screens.why4: The scale is distinct and complete in plain words, including "No difference", which is my likely answer, and "I can't tell" fits as the escape.
screens.why5: No roles or plans leak beyond the named idea, but "your raise go better" drifts from keeping raised cash safe and earning to the fundraising itself.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold after one hearing and a single escape at the end.
screens.instead: Would Palus have been better than where your cash from your last raise sat, or not? A lot better; A little better; No difference; or Worse. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: After I said the idea wouldn't change much on my last raise, it makes obvious sense to ask what would actually help instead.
screens.why2: I get it on first read, but 'keeping the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it' is a long, stiff phrase where I'd just say 'where we park our cash' or 'our treasury setup'.
screens.why3: I run this cash day to day and know what bugs me about it, mostly the operational burden rather than chasing yield, so I can answer from experience.
screens.why4: It is an open box to type in, with no options, rows or chips.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the Palus name I was already shown on the card, but the long job phrase reads like someone else's description pasted in rather than words I would use.
screens.why6: It is one question and can be said, but the second sentence runs well past 20 words and the long middle clause is a mouthful to hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: You said Palus wouldn't change much on your last raise. What would make managing that cash better for you, if anything?

screens.why1: After the card and the questions on whether it would have helped, asking if I'd actually move the money is the obvious next thing, though it comes right after I already said Palus wouldn't make much difference.
screens.why2: I know what treasury means, but 'long-term reserve' isn't a bucket we'd name unless we'd split our cash that way, so I'd have to pause and map it to our own balances.
screens.why3: I run our cash and decide where it sits, so I can say from my own position whether I'd move it out of the bank's treasury product.
screens.why4: The options roughly cover it and the condition on getting cash back fast is the real one, but 'Probably not' and 'No' sit close together and there is no condition for the bigger issue of adding another account and more operational burden.
screens.why5: It's plainly about the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing reads as the founder's internal language or plans beyond the Palus name I've already seen.
screens.why6: It says well as a short list a person can hold, but the stem is two sentences and 'Only if I knew I could get the cash back fast' is a mouthful beside the one-word options.
screens.instead: To use Palus, you'd move some of your reserve cash out of your bank's treasury. Would you do that, or not? Yes; only with fast access to the cash; only if it added little extra work; or no. Or say I can't tell.

screens.why1: I just said I wouldn't move the reserve, so asking what makes it too much trouble is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I get it on first read, but "long-term reserve" isn't how I'd name our cash and "the bank's treasury" sounds slightly off for Mercury's treasury product.
screens.why3: I run these accounts and already chose to avoid extra operational burden even for a higher yield, so I can answer this directly.
screens.why4: It is a box to type in, with no options, rows or chips.
screens.why5: No product name or plan leaks beyond the idea card, but "too much trouble" assumes my reason when I might have said no over safety or yield, and "long-term reserve" is still the idea's framing rather than mine.
screens.why6: It is one short question that says easily and I can answer it after hearing it once.
screens.instead: What's the main reason you wouldn't move that cash out of your bank's treasury?
